title: React page becomes progressively slower after navigation
description: Problem: React page becomes progressively slower after navigation. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: A React application feels fine on first load, but after navigating through five or six pages it becomes noticeably sluggish. Animations stutter, button clicks lag, and the memory indicator in DevTools climbs steadily. This is a classic sign of state or side effects that accumulate with every navigation without being cleaned up.

items: Event listeners attached to window or document are never removed when route components unmount.
Global stores or contexts accumulate subscriptions on every mount without deduplication.
Timers, intervals, or WebSocket connections created in useEffect keep running after navigation.
Large arrays or maps stored in module scope grow every time a user visits a page.
Route transition animations overlap because previous animation frames are not canceled.
Image or data caches in memory are never pruned, so the heap grows until GC pauses become frequent.

terms.definition: A condition where memory is allocated but never released because something still references it.
A brief stop-the-world pause when the JavaScript engine reclaims memory. Frequent pauses cause jank.
A registration to receive updates from an observable, store, or event source. Subscriptions must be unsubscribed when no longer needed.
Any JavaScript task that blocks the main thread for more than fifty milliseconds, causing input delay and frame drops.

data.text: Use the Performance and Memory panels together. Record a trace while navigating through the app, then look for growing heap size and long tasks. If heap size never returns to baseline after navigation, a component is retaining references. If long tasks appear only after several navigations, the accumulated work is finally large enough to block the main thread.

data.title: Treat route components like modals
data.text: Any side effect created in a page component should be torn down when the user leaves the page. If you would clean it up in a modal, you should clean it up in a route component too.

items: Global event buses that emit events to listeners that were never unsubscribed.
React Query or SWR caches that grow without query invalidation or cache time limits.
Canvas or WebGL contexts that are created but never destroyed when a visualization unmounts.
Audio or video elements that keep playing after their component is removed from the DOM.
Intersection observers that observe elements which no longer exist.

cards.description: Return a cleanup function from useEffect to remove listeners and timers.

cards.title: useRef for subscriptions

data.caption: Route navigation lifecycle and leak points
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[User navigates to /dashboard] --> B[Dashboard component mounts]
    B --> C[useEffect starts polling]
    C --> D[User navigates to /settings]
    D --> E[Dashboard component unmounts]
    E --> F{Cleanup ran?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Polling stops]
    F -->|No| H[Polling continues in background]
    H --> I[Memory usage grows]
    I --> J[GC pauses increase]
    J --> K[Jank and slow interactions]
    G --> L[Memory returns to baseline]
    L --> M[Navigation remains fast]

items.question: Why does the app feel fine at first and slow later?
items.answer: A single leaked listener or timer is cheap. After dozens of navigations, the accumulated listeners, timers, or retained objects create enough garbage collection pressure to make every interaction feel sluggish.

items.question: Can React Router cause leaks?
items.answer: React Router itself does not leak, but route components that create side effects without cleanup do. The same rule applies: every mount needs a matching unmount.

items.question: How do I find leaks without a specific reproduction?
items.answer: Navigate through the app repeatedly in a loop while recording heap snapshots in DevTools. Compare snapshots to find object types that grow monotonically. Retainers view will show what is holding them.

data.title: Fix a navigation-related memory leak
data.description: Navigate through an app that leaks memory and fix the root cause.
steps: Open a React app with at least three routes.
Open DevTools Memory panel and take a baseline heap snapshot.
Navigate back and forth between routes twenty times.
Take another snapshot and diff it to find growing object types.
Inspect the retaining path to identify the leaking component.
Add cleanup and verify the heap stabilizes.
data.expectedOutcome: After the fix, repeated navigation should not increase retained heap size, and the app should remain responsive regardless of route count.

data.title: Summary
points: Progressive slowness after navigation is almost always a leak or accumulated side effect.
Use DevTools heap snapshots to confirm growing retained memory.
Always return a cleanup function from useEffect for listeners, timers, and subscriptions.
Abort in-flight requests on unmount to prevent state updates on unmounted components.
Validate by repeating the navigation flow and confirming the heap stabilizes
data.takeaway: A senior engineer treats every mount as a contract: if you acquire a resource in useEffect, you must release it in the cleanup function before the component leaves the screen.
